subtitle: See how shared assumptions become the rules, forms, timelines and resources that carry norms forward, and use systems thinking and a structural lens to find where a change would make a lasting difference.
audience: For all DHS and DSD staff, supervisors and leaders, especially those who design or maintain forms, procedures, timelines, contracts or budgets. This is Module 2 of the Culture, Power, and Organizational Norms path; Module 1 is helpful background.

lessons.title: From habit to structure
objectives: Explain how a cultural assumption becomes part of a rule, form, timeline or budget.
Distinguish event, pattern and structural explanations of a recurring problem.
Explain why structural explanations point toward more durable changes.
Describe one recurring problem at all three levels of explanation.
lessons.teaching:
Module 1 described culture as the shared assumptions a group learned while dealing with its problems. This module follows those assumptions one step further, into the systems an organization builds. When a team decides once that a request must arrive in writing, someone eventually designs a form. When a unit settles into a certain pace, the pace becomes a timeline in a procedure. When leaders believe that a particular kind of expertise is what solves problems, the budget funds that expertise. At each step an assumption becomes something concrete, and the concrete thing keeps working whether or not anyone still holds the assumption.

Schein observed that a solution which works long enough becomes an assumption that is taken for granted and stops being open to debate. Systems make that process durable. A form outlasts the person who designed it. A timeline written into a procedure continues after the reasons for it are forgotten. New staff learn the system as simply how the work is done, and the assumption passes on without ever being stated. None of this is a sign of bad faith. It is how organizations remember. The difficulty is that a system remembers the conditions of the past, while the people using it live in the present.

Peter Senge's writing on learning organizations offers a useful way to see this. Senge distinguished three kinds of explanation for what happens in an organization. Event explanations focus on who did what to whom, and Senge argued that they keep people in a reactive stance toward change. Pattern-of-behavior explanations look for longer-term trends and what they imply. Structural explanations ask what causes the patterns, and Senge called them the most powerful, because only they address the underlying causes of behavior at a level where patterns can be changed. In public service terms, an event explanation says that a family missed a deadline. A pattern explanation notices that families in a certain situation miss that deadline often. A structural explanation asks how the deadline, the delivery method, the form and the staffing combine to produce that result.

Each level of explanation leads to a different kind of response. Events invite individual fixes: a reminder call, a one-time extension, a corrective conversation. Those may help one person and leave the pattern untouched. Structural explanations invite changes to the system itself, such as a different way of delivering a notice, a revised form or a different use of staff time, which affect everyone who goes through the process. Structural thinking does not erase individual responsibility, and it does not replace the formal routes for concerns about someone's conduct, which belong with Human Resources or the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division. It adds a question that individual fixes cannot answer: what in the design keeps producing this result?
lessons.keyPoint: Assumptions become rules, forms, timelines and budgets, and those systems keep the assumptions working after people forget them. Ask what in the design keeps producing a result, not only who was involved.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{CASE_MANAGER}} brings a concern to a team meeting. Over the past several months, a number of people on the caseload have had services paused because a renewal packet was not returned on time. Each time, the team treated it as a one-off: a phone call, an extension, a note in the file. {{SUPERVISOR}} asks the team to look at the situation differently.
lessons.question: Which question best moves the team toward a structural explanation?
choices: Which staff member should have followed up sooner in each case?
How many packets were late this month compared with last month?
How do the packet's timeline, delivery method, format and our follow-up steps combine, and who do they work least well for?
feedback: This is an event explanation. It may matter for a single case, but it keeps the team reactive and leaves the design unexamined.
Counting helps the team see a pattern, but it does not ask what is producing the pattern.
This asks what in the system keeps producing the result and for whom, which points toward changes that would help everyone who uses the process.
lessons.reflection: Privately think of a problem in your work that keeps coming back despite repeated fixes, or use the practice case. How have you usually explained it: as events, as a pattern, or as a structure? What would a structural explanation add?
lessons.action: Choose one recurring problem in your area. Write one sentence explaining it at each level: event, pattern and structure. Note one feature of the structure, such as a form, a timeline or a staffing arrangement, and who owns it.

check.question: In Senge's account, why are structural explanations the most powerful?
check.correct: They address the underlying causes of behavior at a level where patterns can be changed.
wrong: They identify the person responsible for a problem more quickly.
They remove the need to gather information about events and patterns.
check.feedback: Structural explanations ask what causes the patterns. They build on what events and patterns show rather than skipping them, and their purpose is to find causes in the design, not to assign individual fault.

lessons.title: Defaults: where norms hide in rules, forms, timelines and resources
objectives: Define a default and explain how it carries a norm forward.
Identify defaults in four places: rules, forms, timelines and resources.
Connect defaults to Senge's idea of mental models.
Trace where one default came from and who can change it.
lessons.teaching:
A default is what happens when no one makes a different choice. It is the option already selected, the field that must be filled in, the meeting time that repeats every week, the budget line that rolls over each year. Defaults are powerful because they do not feel like decisions. They feel like the starting point. Yet every default was a decision at some point, and each one carries an assumption about who the typical person is and what the typical situation looks like.

Defaults appear in at least four places in public service work. Rules and procedures set defaults about what is required, such as a signature in a particular form or a single accepted type of document. Forms set defaults about who the user is: the language they read, the records they keep, whether they have a fixed address, a personal phone or an email account, and how their household is arranged. Timelines set defaults about how quickly people can respond, often fitting someone with predictable hours, reliable mail and no need for an interpreter or support person. Resources set defaults through what gets funded and staffed, such as whether interpretation or alternative formats are planned and budgeted from the start or requested later as exceptions. When a default fits most staff and many users, the people it does not fit do extra work to reach the same result, and that extra work is easy for everyone else to miss.

Senge described the assumptions people carry about how the world works as mental models, and Senge noted that new ideas often stall because they conflict with established mental models. Defaults can be understood as mental models built into systems. If a team's picture of a typical applicant is someone who reads English comfortably and can take calls during business hours, the form and the timeline will be designed for that person, and the design will keep teaching that picture to every new staff member who learns the process. Changing the default usually requires surfacing the mental model behind it first, which is why the Module 1 habit of naming assumptions tentatively matters here as well.

A practical habit is to trace a default back to its source. Ask whether a requirement comes from federal or state law, from administrative rule, from DHS or division policy, from a contract, or from a past decision that became habit. Ask who owns it and who could authorize a change. Many defaults are necessary and should stay. Some can be changed within a unit's own authority. Others need a policy owner, legal review or a different decision maker. Tracing the source protects a team from two opposite errors: treating a habit as if it were law, and treating a legal requirement as if it were a preference. When one person needs an exception, such as an accommodation, that request goes through the established process rather than an informal workaround.
lessons.keyPoint: Every default was once a decision, and it carries an assumption about the typical person. Trace each default to its source and owner before deciding whether it should change.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is updating an online request form. The current version requires an email address, is offered only in English, and ends a session after fifteen minutes without activity. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}}, who previously worked at a county front desk, mentions that many people they helped shared a phone with family, used a library computer, or needed a support person to help them complete forms.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} do with this information?
choices: Trace each of the three defaults to its source and owner, then ask people who use the form, and staff who help them, which defaults create the most difficulty.
Keep the form as it is, since people who need help can always call.
Remove all three features right away without checking whether any of them are required.
feedback: This separates requirements from habits, involves the people affected, and gives the team evidence for deciding what to change and who must approve it.
A phone option may help some people, but it leaves the defaults in place and shifts extra work onto the people the form fits least.
The concern is valid, but some defaults may have security, legal or technical reasons behind them. Checking the source keeps the change sound and within the team's authority.
lessons.reflection: Privately notice one default in a tool or process you use every day, such as a template, a required field or a standard timeline. Who does it seem designed for? Who might need to do extra work to meet it?
lessons.action: Pick one default in your work, in a rule, form, timeline or resource. Write what it assumes about the typical person, where it comes from (law, rule, policy, contract or habit), and who could authorize a change.

check.question: Which of these best describes a default?
check.correct: What happens when no one makes a different choice, which carries an earlier decision's assumptions forward.
wrong: A requirement that is always set by law and cannot be changed.
A mistake staff make when they skip a step.
check.feedback: Defaults are earlier decisions that now feel like the starting point. Some come from law and many do not, which is why tracing the source matters before deciding what to do.

lessons.title: A structural lens: people are situated differently
objectives: Explain the idea that people are situated differently within the same structures.
Describe targeted universalism as universal goals pursued through targeted strategies.
Explain how a single universal strategy can leave some groups behind.
Apply the five steps of targeted universalism to a practice goal.
lessons.teaching:
A structural lens starts from a simple observation: the same rule meets people in different situations. john a. powell, who directs the Othering and Belonging Institute at the University of California, Berkeley, and co-authors Stephen Menendian and Wendy Ake write that individuals are necessarily situated within structures and systems, and that structures are not neutral. A process designed around one kind of household, schedule or set of resources will work smoothly for people in that situation and less well for others, even when every staff member applies it the same way. The lens does not ask whether anyone meant to exclude someone. It asks how the structure interacts with the situations people are actually in.

In a 2019 primer published by what was then called the Haas Institute for a Fair and Inclusive Society, the three authors describe an approach they call targeted universalism. In their words, it means setting universal goals pursued by targeted processes to achieve those goals. The goal applies to everyone, while the strategies differ according to how groups are situated in relation to structures, culture and geography. The authors argue that a universal strategy on its own is likely to be indifferent to the reality that different groups are situated differently, and that universal approaches can widen disparities when they address only one barrier. Their example is Massachusetts' universal health insurance law, which raised coverage overall but did not address barriers such as provider shortages, transportation or language, and the authors report that racial disparities in coverage widened. In their phrase, the single strategy moved some people to the goal and left others behind.

The primer lays out five steps. Establish a universal goal grounded in a broadly shared problem and shared aspirations. Assess how the general population is doing against the goal. Identify the groups and places that are doing differently, which requires data broken down in meaningful ways. Assess the structures that support or impede each group in reaching the goal, including missing supports and not only active obstacles. Then develop and carry out targeted strategies so that each group can reach the goal. For a DSD team, a universal goal might be that every eligible person can complete a service request within a reasonable time. Targeted strategies might include different ways of delivering notices, interpretation planned from the start, or support for people who use assistive technology, all aimed at the same goal.

This framing helps with a common objection. Some colleagues worry that targeted strategies mean lowering standards for some people or giving others an unfair advantage. Targeted universalism answers that the goal and the standard stay the same for everyone; what changes is the path, because starting conditions differ. That is a design argument, not a legal test. Questions about eligibility, civil rights or whether a particular strategy is permitted belong to the responsible office and to legal counsel, and data broken down by group must be handled under data privacy and disclosure requirements. The structural lens is a way of asking better questions about a system. It is one approach among several, and its value in a given case depends on the evidence and on what the people affected say about their experience.
lessons.keyPoint: Structures are not neutral; people meet the same rule from different situations. Targeted universalism keeps one goal for everyone and designs different paths to reach it.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team sets a goal that every person approved for a service receives a clear explanation of next steps within two weeks. Overall, most people do. When {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} looks more closely, people who need an interpreter, people without a stable mailing address, and people who rely on a support person to read their mail are less likely to have received a usable explanation in time. {{SUPERVISOR}} suggests that the team simply try harder with everyone.
lessons.question: How could the team apply a targeted universalism approach?
choices: Lower the two-week goal for the groups that are not meeting it, since their situations are harder.
Keep the same goal, examine the structures that affect each group, such as mail, language and reading support, and design specific strategies for each while tracking progress toward the shared goal.
Treat everyone exactly the same and send the explanation again by mail.
feedback: Changing the goal for some groups abandons the shared standard. Targeted universalism keeps the goal and changes the strategy.
This keeps one standard for everyone, looks at how each group is situated, and designs different paths to the same goal.
Repeating a single strategy addresses one barrier at most and is likely to leave the same groups behind.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider one goal your team works toward for everyone. Who seems to reach it easily, and who has a harder path because of how they are situated? You do not need data to reflect, but note what data would help you see more clearly.
lessons.action: Choose one goal your team holds for everyone. Walk briefly through the five steps: state the universal goal, note what you know about overall performance, list groups or places that may differ, name one structure that affects each, and suggest one targeted strategy. Note what data you would need and who handles it under privacy rules.

check.question: What does targeted universalism keep the same for everyone?
check.correct: The goal, while the strategies for reaching it are tailored to how groups are situated.
wrong: The strategy, so that no group receives anything different.
Nothing, because each group sets its own goal.
check.feedback: The approach pairs a universal goal with targeted processes. Identical strategies can leave some groups behind, and separate goals give up the shared standard.

lessons.title: Where to intervene, and how to know it helped
objectives: Describe leverage points as places in a system where a change has more or less effect.
Explain why changing information flows, rules and goals usually matters more than adjusting numbers.
Connect leverage to decision rights and to the DHS Equity Policy.
Plan a small test of a system change and how to learn from it.
lessons.teaching:
Once a team can see how assumptions live in systems, the next question is where to act. Donella Meadows, a systems scientist, wrote a widely cited essay listing places to intervene in a system in increasing order of effectiveness. Near the bottom are constants, parameters and numbers, such as a standard or an amount. Meadows wrote that parameters come dead last on the essay's list of powerful interventions, because changing them rarely changes behavior. Higher on the list are the structure of information flows, meaning who does and does not have access to information; the rules of the system; the goals of the system; and, near the top, the mindset or paradigm out of which the system arises.

That ordering matches what many public service teams experience. Extending a deadline by three days is a parameter change. It may help and is often worth doing, but the pattern frequently returns. Making sure a support person receives a copy of a notice, when the person has authorized it, changes an information flow. Changing what a procedure requires is a rule change. Changing what a team measures itself against, for example from packets processed to people who completed the process with what they needed, is a goal change. Meadows also wrote that power over the rules is real power, and that understanding the deepest problems in a system means paying attention to the rules and to who has power over them.

That observation connects leverage to decision rights. A team may see a high-leverage change and still lack the authority to make it. Mapping who owns each rule, form, timeline and resource, as described in Lesson 2, tells a team which changes it can test now and which it needs to bring to a policy owner, to leadership or for legal review. The DHS Equity Policy directs staff to consider equity in their daily work and to use the agency's equity analysis toolkit for decisions across policy, budgets, procurement, hiring and service delivery. The State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit asks who is affected, how they are meaningfully engaged and how equity impacts will be reviewed. These are the agency's own tools for bringing a structural question to the people who can act on it, and an optional exercise in this course does not replace them.

Changing a system is a cycle rather than a single act. Plan a small change with the people it affects, try it, study what happened, and adjust. Decide in advance what would show that the change helped, and watch for unintended effects. In this path, success is measured by changes in the work, such as a clearer notice, a fairer decision, a barrier removed, or community input that led to a documented change, rather than by how many people finished a course. Module 3 adds another lens for noticing the norms behind systems: Tema Okun's characteristics, such as a sense of urgency and perfectionism, presented with both the framework's strengths and the critiques of it. The modules after that apply the same thinking to accessibility, belonging and action.
lessons.keyPoint: Adjusting numbers rarely changes a pattern; changing information flows, rules and goals often does. Know who holds power over the rule, test small changes with the people affected, and measure success in the work.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team has extended a response deadline twice, and late responses keep returning at about the same level. {{SUPERVISOR}} proposes a third extension. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, a county partner, notes that many people do not see the notice until a support person visits, and suggests that a copy could go to the support person when the person authorizes it. {{CASE_MANAGER}} points out that the team measures timeliness but not whether people understood what they needed to do.
lessons.question: Which plan uses leverage best?
choices: Extend the deadline again, since the earlier extensions were partly successful.

Bring the information-flow change and a new measure of understanding to the procedure's owner, propose a small test with people who have authorized it, and set a date to review the results with the county partner.
Change the procedure on the team's own authority, since the problem is obvious.
feedback: A parameter change may bring short-term relief, but the pattern has returned twice. It does not address why people miss the notice.
This targets an information flow and the team's goal, respects decision rights and privacy, and builds in a way to learn whether the change helped.
The idea may be sound, but acting outside the team's authority can create new problems, including privacy problems, and skips the owner who can make the change last.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a change you or your team made that did not last, or use the practice case. Was it a change to a number, an information flow, a rule or a goal? What might a higher-leverage change have looked like?
lessons.action: For one recurring problem, list one possible change at each of four levels: a number, an information flow, a rule and a goal. Identify who owns each one, choose one you can test or propose, and write down how you will know whether it helped and when you will look again.

check.question: According to Meadows, why is changing a parameter such as a deadline often a low-leverage intervention?
check.correct: Parameter changes rarely change the behavior of the system, so the underlying pattern tends to return.
wrong: Parameters are set by law and can never be changed.
Parameter changes always make a problem worse.
check.feedback: Meadows placed parameters last among powerful interventions because they seldom change behavior. They can still help in the short term, many of them can be changed, and they are not harmful by nature.

cards.back: Senge's three kinds of explanation: who did what, what trends recur, and what causes the trends. Structural explanations address causes at a level where patterns can change.
What happens when no one makes a different choice. Every default was once a decision, and it carries that decision's assumptions forward.
The assumptions people carry about how the world works. When they are built into forms, rules and timelines, they keep teaching new staff the same picture.
People are situated differently within the same structures, and structures are not neutral (powell, Menendian and Ake).
Setting universal goals pursued by targeted processes to achieve those goals. The goal stays the same for everyone; the paths differ.
A place in a system where a change has more or less effect. In Meadows's list, numbers are low; information flows, rules, goals and mindsets are higher.
A small, repeated test cycle for changing a system with the people it affects. Success is measured by changes in the work.

aid.heading: Explain the problem at three levels
items: Event: what happened, and to whom.
Pattern: how often it happens, and for whom.
Structure: which rules, forms, timelines and resources combine to produce the pattern.
Ask what in the design keeps producing the result.

aid.heading: Trace the defaults
items: List the defaults in the rule, form, timeline and resources involved.
Write what each default assumes about the typical person.
Find whether each comes from law, rule, policy, contract or habit, and who owns it.
Route individual exceptions, such as accommodations, through the established process.

aid.heading: Apply a structural lens
items: State one universal goal for everyone.
Identify who is situated differently in relation to the goal.
Name the structures that support or impede each group, including missing supports.
Design targeted strategies toward the same goal, and handle data broken down by group under privacy rules.

aid.heading: Choose where to intervene
items: List possible changes to a number, an information flow, a rule and a goal.
Identify who holds power over each rule, and bring changes outside your authority to that owner.
Use the DHS Equity Policy and the Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions they cover.
Plan, try, study and adjust, and look for the result in the work itself.

sources.title: Peter M. Senge, The Leader's New Work: Building Learning Organizations, Sloan Management Review 32, no. 1 (Fall 1990)
sources.note: Supports the distinction between event, pattern-of-behavior and structural explanations, the statement that structural explanations are the most powerful, and the description of mental models that conflict with new ideas (lessons 1 and 2). Read in the publisher's PDF view. A conceptual article drawn from The Fifth Discipline, not an empirical study.

sources.title: Edgar H. Schein, Organizational Culture: A Dynamic Model, MIT Sloan School of Management Working Paper 1412-83 (February 1983), DSpace@MIT
sources.note: Supports the observation that a value or solution that keeps working becomes a taken-for-granted assumption no longer open to debate (lesson 1). The step from assumptions into forms, timelines and budgets is the course's own application.

sources.title: john a. powell, Stephen Menendian and Wendy Ake, Targeted Universalism: Policy and Practice, Haas Institute for a Fair and Inclusive Society, University of California, Berkeley (May 2019)
sources.note: Supports the definition of targeted universalism, the five steps, the statements that individuals are situated within structures and that structures are not neutral, and the Massachusetts health coverage example (lesson 3). The institute now operates as the Othering and Belonging Institute. A policy primer, not a legal standard; the DSD examples are the course's own.

sources.title: Donella Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (The Donella Meadows Project)
sources.note: Supports the ordered list of places to intervene, the statement that parameters rarely change behavior, the placement of information flows, rules, goals and paradigms higher on the list, and the remark that power over the rules is real power (lesson 4). A reflective essay by a systems scientist, not an empirical test of the ordering.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency policy on considering equity in daily work and using the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions across policy, budgets, procurement, hiring and service delivery (lesson 4). This course is learning material, not a substitute for the policy.

sources.title: State of Minnesota, Equity Analysis Toolkit
sources.note: A state-government resource for asking who is affected, engaging people meaningfully, and reviewing equity impacts in a decision (lesson 4).

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.05 — Duties of responsible authority
sources.note: Data collection, use and disclosure duties apply to mapping and analysis, including data broken down by group (lessons 3 and 4); removing names does not automatically make information public.
